articles.title: How Often Should You Replace Running Shoes? Podiatrists Explain
articles.summary: Running in worn-out shoes can lead to aches, pains and injuries. Podiatrists break down how many miles your running shoes should last and when it’s time for a new pair.
articles.body: We don’t always have the answers, but we have some people on speed dial who do — which is why we present to you our series FYI where we have experts explain if hair removal cream is actually bad, how often you should change your towels and more. Running shoes don’t last forever, even if they still look fine from the outside. Over time, the cushioning and support inside break down and running in shoes that have lost their structure can leave your feet, knees and joints unsupported, making you more prone to aches, pains and even injuries. The tricky part is that this breakdown happens gradually, so it’s easy to keep running in shoes that have quietly stopped doing their job. To find out exactly when it’s time to retire your running shoes — and what to watch for before your body starts sending its own warning signals — I talked to doctors who explained how mileage and body type factor into the equation. I’ve also rounded up some podiatrist- and editor-approved running shoes worth adding to your cart if you find that it’s time for a fresh pair. How often do running shoes need to be replaced? Most doctors say mileage is the clearest benchmark for retiring your running shoes. “In general, a running shoe should last somewhere between 300 and 500 miles,” says Dr. Dietmar Walter, head of podiatry at Stride Soles, a custom orthotics company. “However, the exact length depends on your weight, running surface and of course the shoe type.” Treadmills tend to be gentler on shoes, while consistently running on pavement or concrete can wear down cushioning a bit faster, since there’s less natural give to absorb the impact. Body weight in particular can make a dramatic difference in how quickly a shoe wears out. “I see many patients over 200 pounds only last 200 miles in their shoes, while someone under 140 pounds might last over 550 miles,” says Walter. That’s a gap of more than 350 miles between the two groups, underscoring why there’s no single mileage number that works for every runner — and why paying attention to how your shoes feel matters just as much as counting miles. What are signs you need to replace your running shoes? Mileage is a helpful guideline, but your body often sends signals before you hit a specific number. “A good sign that your shoes need replacing is if you are starting to get unexpected aches and pains — like achilles tendonitis, shin splints or plantar fascia pain,” says Dr. Milica McDowell, a doctor of physical therapy and co-author of Walk: Rediscover the Most Natural Way to Boost Your Health and Longevity ― One Step at a Time. If new discomfort starts creeping in during or after your runs, it’s worth taking a closer look at your shoes before the problem gets worse. Walter also says you can examine your shoe to look for signs of excessive wear. These are the things he says point to your shoes needing to be replaced: Look at the midsole: If it looks compressed, has striations (grooves or ridges) in it or has uneven wear, it’s likely time to replace the shoes.Check the inside back of your shoes: Look at where your achilles rests against the back of your shoes. If that area is torn or there is missing material, this is a major sign to replace your shoe as your foot is no longer being held securely as you run.Examine the bottom of your shoes: Simply checking the rubber at the bottom of your shoes is an easy way to see if there is excessive wear. If you notice foam through the bottom or areas where there is no tread, it’s likely time to replace your shoes. The breathable mesh upper offers a comfortable, snug fit, while the durable rubber outsole delivers reliable traction — making it a solid, everyday pick for runners logging daily miles. articles.title: 9/11 victim's identity emerges nearly 25 years later after DNA breakthrough cracks mystery
articles.summary: A first-of-its-kind forensic genealogy technique helped New York City investigators identify a World Trade Center victim nearly 25 years after 9/11.
articles.body: Nearly 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks, a family has finally received an answer after New York City investigators used a first-of-its-kind DNA and genealogy technique to identify a woman killed at the World Trade Center. The adult woman, whose name is being withheld at her family’s request, is the first World Trade Center victim identified through forensic investigative genetic genealogy, New York City officials announced Sunday. Her identification marks the 1,654th person identified from remains recovered after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, which killed 2,753 people in New York City. 9/11 MUSEUM CEO REFLECTS ON LASTING IMPACT OF TERROR ATTACKS AS AMERICA MARKS 250TH BIRTHDAY The breakthrough came through a collaboration between the Office of Chief Medical Examiner, and the NYPD’s Investigative Genetic Genealogy Squad. The technique pairs specialized DNA analysis with genealogy research to generate leads that are then confirmed through forensic testing. "As we approach the 25th anniversary of the horrific September 11 attacks, we honor the nearly 3,000 people whose lives were stolen that day," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement. "We remain committed to the families who have spent 25 years waiting for answers." REMAINS FOUND IN UTAH DESERT 28 YEARS AGO WITH HELP OF A PSYCHIC FINALLY IDENTIFIED THROUGH DNA GENEALOGY Forensic investigative genetic genealogy has emerged as a powerful tool in cold cases, allowing investigators to trace family connections from DNA evidence and identify people who may otherwise have remained unknown. Chief Medical Examiner Dr. Graham said the new method could help advance the city’s long-running effort to identify those killed in the attacks. WOMAN FOUND IN SHALLOW GRAVE ID’D AFTER 44 YEARS AS MILLIONAIRE TIED TO ESTATE MURDER PLOT "This sacred commitment is propelled by our dedication to apply the most innovative scientific techniques," Graham said. "FIGG represents a promising new addition to our toolkit." Officials said they are also using renewed family outreach and continued DNA retesting to link recovered remains to victims already identified. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But the work remains unfinished. About 1,099 World Trade Center victims, roughly 40% of those killed, have yet to be identified. The woman is the first newly identified World Trade Center victim since August 2025, officials said.

articles.title: 'What women wears is her choice':  Rahul Gandhi backs Kriti Sanon over Raksha Bandhan ad row
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi on Tuesday defended actor Kriti Sanon amid criticism of her outfit in a Raksha Bandhan a.

articles.title: Who does Iran trade with and what could Trump's 'economic D-Day' mean?
articles.summary: Iran is no stranger to US sanctions and has developed deep economic ties with several countries.
articles.body:
The US has said "the single greatest financial offensive ever" will help it and Israel end their ongoing war with Iran.

However, Iran is no stranger to these tactics.

The regime has faced near continuous US sanctions since the Islamic Revolution of 1979. In that time, it has developed deep trade ties with several countries which either have a history of ignoring US economic pressure themselves or cannot afford to stop trading with Iran.

As a result, Iran says it is "fully prepared" for the new US sanctions and many economists argue the impact of Washington's latest move will be limited.

So, who does Iran trade with? And could what the US has called an "economic D-Day" have any real impact on Iran?

China is the biggest buyer of Iranian goods, making up 26.9% of its exports in 2025, according data from the International Trade Centre (ITC), a subsidiary of the United Nations and the World Trade Organisation.

There a few caveats to ITC's data, which covers a period before the US-Israel war with Iran began.

First, several economists believe that even before the conflict started, a lot of Iranian oil sales, particularly to China, were underreported for political reasons.

Second, the ITC tallies Iran's exports using mostly the import numbers reported by its trading partners - owing to the difficulty in getting up to date export data from Iran.

Third, import data for some of Iran's trading partners, such as Iraq, is incomplete.

Despite this, Iranian trade's importance to China is clear from its response to the US announcement of "economic D-Day".

It said that it was firmly opposed to what it called "illegal unilateral sanctions", that economic pressure tactics would not help resolve problems and that Beijing would safeguard its own interests.

Turkey is another large trading partner of Iran, according to ITC data, but it has a much friendlier relationship with the US than China.

This puts it in a challenging position. The US has threatened to punish those who continue to trade with Iran as part of its economic pressure tactics.

However, economists point out that Turkey cannot stop trading with it without significant damage to its economy, which is already struggling with inflation running at 31.8%, according to official data .

In short, as the only Nato member to share a border with Iran, Turkey has to balance its relationship with military allies and maintaining a relationship with its close economic neighbour.

Like Turkey, Pakistan borders Iran and is one of its biggest export partners, according to ITC data, while also being keen to maintain a good relationship with the US.

But unlike Turkey, Pakistan's top export partner is instead the US, meaning it has more to lose from any economic punishment imposed by Washington.

It is also a key mediator in peace talks between the US and Iran, meaning a breakdown in its relationship with either country could make finding a solution to the conflict even more challenging.

The other complicating factor is that not all of Pakistan's trade with Iran is within the Pakistan government's control.

The BBC has seen evidence that oil is being smuggled across the border from Iran to Pakistan en masse by bikers , some as young as 15.

This was the case before the Iran war began, but data suggests the practice has picked up since.

And though the US and Pakistan's oil firms have pressured Pakistan's government to clamp down on the practice, it has struggled to police remote parts of the 900km border.

The BBC has previously asked the Iranian government to comment on the allegation that it is involved in the fuel smuggling. It did not respond.

Armenia is another major trading partner of Iran, according to the ITC data.

Where it differs the most from others is that its top export partner is Russia, which accounts for 34.9% of all goods sold by Armenia in 2025.

This is despite the fact that Russia has faced sanctions from the US and its allies since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

This suggests Armenia may be willing to continue trading with Iran despite mounting US pressure.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the sanctions against Iran will "tighten the noose and block every potential source of revenue".

Yet, many experts disagree. Advisory firm Oxford Economics said the direct impact on Iran's revenues would be "somewhat of a damp squib".

Ali Vaez, deputy director at the International Crisis Group, said: "Anything that moves in Iran has already been sanctioned by multiple layers of sanctions, in fact.

"So the question now is one of enforcement. Does the United States have what it takes to impose fines and levies on countries that continue to trade with Iran?"

He noted how the US started an economic war with China, Iran's biggest trading partner, last year but "backed out of it".

Former senior advisor at the state department Aya Ibrahim said the US's overreliance on them "incentivises countries to find ways around that system".

She also raised concerns that the sanctions may have the biggest affect on people, rather than economies, as they "deny people necessities to stay alive".

Meanwhile, global markets have had a muted response to the announcement.

Global oil prices fell following the announcement, but are still far higher than pre-war levels.

Stock traders were even less moved by the news, with the major indexes of the biggest companies listed in the US, Europe, and Asia barely shifting.

The US will has a way to go before it convinces economists, investors, and the nations trading with Iran that its sanctions threat is to be taken seriously.

articles.title: Trump says Strait of Hormuz has been demined, warns Iran not to plant more
articles.summary: Aug 25 (Reuters) - U.S.
articles.body:
Aug 25 (Reuters) - U.S. President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that all mines ‌had been detonated or removed from international ‌waters of the Strait of Hormuz and that Iran ​has been told that any ship or boat placing new mines will be destroyed.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump said the United ‌States, through its ⁠Space Force, was watching "every square inch" of the Strait, a key waterway ⁠in the global energy supply chain.

"There is a Zero Tolerance policy on mine placement in ​full ​force and effect," Trump ​said.

The U.S. and ‌Iran have not conducted air strikes on each other's militaries for weeks, but attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have continued as the two sides vie for control ‌of the narrow maritime passage.

Oil ​transits through the strait ​were at 5 ​million barrels per day on ‌Monday, provisional data from shiptracker ​Vortexa showed, ​down from more than 20 million per day before the war or about one ​of every ‌five barrels consumed worldwide.

articles.title: What Are Weight Loss Patches, and Do They Work?
articles.summary: Weight loss patches pop up online, but are they safe and do they work? Here’s what experts have to say.
articles.body:

It's tempting to start searching for extra help if you've tried to lose weight but haven't had much success. While GLP-1 medications are slowly becoming more affordable and accessible, their still-hefty price tag puts them out of reach for many. With that, you may be curious about whether weight loss patches could help you achieve your goals.

Meet the experts : Jessica Cording, R.D., is author of The Little Book of Game Changers ; Keri Gans, R.D., is author of The Small Change Diet ; Gina Keatley, C.D.N., is co-owner of Keatley Medical Nutrition Therapy ; Mir Ali, M.D ., is the medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California; Ife J. Rodney, M.D ., is founding director of Eternal Dermatology + Aesthetics

These stickers come in a range of prices, but they're still a fraction of the cost of list-price GLP-1s and can be purchased without seeing a doctors, making them understandably appealing. They go by names like "GLP-1 patches," "fit patches," and "slimming patches," and are small enough to hide under your clothes.

But what are weight loss patches and, more importantly, do they work? Simply put, doctors are wary—for a bunch of reasons. Consider this your primer before adding weight loss patches to your cart.

Weight loss patches are bandages that contain certain ingredients the manufacturers claim will help the wearer lose weight. Once the adhesive patches are applied, they're supposed to transfer the ingredients to your body over time.

There are different weight loss patches on the market, including some that contain a little ball of ingredients that goes inside your belly button (and are held in place by the adhesive).

What do weight loss patches claim to do?

Each weight loss patch has slightly different claims, but the overarching idea is that they can help you lose weight. Some patches promise to " boost metabolism ," " curb cravings ," and " burn excess fat ." At least one claims to block fat absorption in the body.

While some patches say that they're backed by science, they don't actually show the research.

These patches are considered supplements and therefore aren't tightly regulated by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). As a result, it's hard to know for sure what is in them, points out Jessica Cording, R.D., author of The Little Book of Game Changers . However, the following ingredients come up often with weight loss patches:

Acai . Acai is a type of fruit that is "packed with antioxidants which may lead to decreased inflammation in the body," says Keri Gans, R.D., author of The Small Change Diet . "However, believing that leads to weight loss when absorbed through the skin is not scientifically proven at all," she adds.

Green coffee extract . This is "basically coffee beans that haven't been roasted," Cording says, adding that there's "not a lot of research on them and weight loss." Green coffee extract "has been associated with a decrease in fat cells and increase in energy" when it's eaten, Gans says. But, she adds, "it's not even conclusively proven" to help you lose weight when it's ingested and certainly not proven when it's applied to your skin.

Garcinia cambogia . Garcinia cambogia is believed to suppress appetite, but is not scientifically proven to work, Gans says. Cording calls this ingredient a "big red flag," noting that it's been associated with liver toxicity.

Berberine . This plant compound has been dubbed " nature's Ozempic ." While it's been linked with modest weight loss, it's unclear what kind of effect, if any, it would have in a patch form.

Ultimately, "weight loss patches can have any kind of variable substance in them," says Mir Ali, M.D ., medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California. "I just haven't seen convincing evidence that any of these work," he adds.

It's difficult to say with certainty what the side effects can be from weight loss patches, given that it's hard to know what's actually in them, Cording says. However, experts say a few things could happen.

"With the patches, the body may not be able to absorb any benefit from these food products," says Gina Keatley, C.D.N., co-owner Keatley Medical Nutrition Therapy . "Our skin is not great at absorbing stuff—which is a good thing—but to increase absorption, some manufacturers may use chemicals that help bring 'stuff' through the skin and into the bloodstream." This, she says, is dangerous because your skin's protective barrier can't differentiate between good nutrients and things like harmful heavy metals.

Also, if you're on any medications, Gans says that there's a chance using a weight loss patch could interfere with your medication's effectiveness.

How do weight loss patches impact your skin?

This is a valid question, given that these patches literally stick onto your skin. The potential impact of these patches on your skin largely depends on what's in them, says Ife J. Rodney, M.D ., founding director of Eternal Dermatology + Aesthetics.

But sticking anything regularly to your skin can cause issues, she says. "The contact of those substances on your skin can cause contact dermatitis irritation," Dr. Rodney says. "It can also increase sweat and irritation in the area." What's more, the potential for irritation may be greater if you keep applying patches to the same spot.

Experts say there's really no data to support using these. Keatley strongly discourages people from using weight loss patches. "Ask yourself, why patches?" she says. "If your life is so hectic that the only way to get weight loss is a patch, then you may be very, very out of balance."

Instead, she suggests taking three days to track your meals. "See if you're eating too little or too much and start there," she says. "Skip the patches."

Cording also recommends taking a pass on using weight loss patches. "They are so ridiculous," she says. "These are not a reliable weight-loss option."

Because so little is known about weight loss patches and what's in them, it's difficult to say that they're safe. "Best case scenario is we don't have research to support that they work," Cording says. Worst case, depending on their ingredients, they may cause serious effects to your health.

Dr. Ali agrees. "We have no data to suggest that these are safe or that they work," he says.

Weight loss patches vs. GLP-1 medications

There is a big difference between weight loss patches and GLP-1 medications beyond price tag. GLP-1 medications like semaglutide and tirzepatide have been rigorously studied in clinical trials, suggesting that they're safe and effective to use for weight loss, Dr. Ali points out. "Weight loss patches have not been through any of that," he says.

GLP-1 medications also work through specific pathways in your body to tamp down cravings, lower feelings of hunger, and slow digestion, Dr. Ali explains. It's unclear if weight loss patches can achieve any of that, he says.

What to do if you're considering using weight loss patches

Experts universally agree that weight loss patches are not a good idea, and may even be dangerous for your health. If you're tempted to use weight loss patches, Dr. Ali recommends consulting with a healthcare professional first.

"Talk about what your goals are," he says. "If you have significant weight to lose, there are much better tools available—dietary counseling, medications, even surgery."

Dr. Ali says it's "not realistic" to expect big changes from sticking a patch on your skin. "It's really important to focus on changing your eating habits and eating the right things," he says. And, if that's not effective for you, it's time to rope in a professional for personalized guidance.

articles.title: Did India hit Kirana Hills during Op Sindoor? Ex-CDS Anil Chauhan clears air
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: Former Chief of Defence Staff Anil Chauhan on Tuesday said India may have hit Pakistan's Kirana Hills during Operation Sindoor last year, b.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Former Chief of Defence Staff Anil Chauhan on Tuesday said India may have hit Pakistan's Kirana Hills during Operation Sindoor last year, but the strike was unintentional.Speaking at the âVIMARSHâ event on Operation Sindoor and its aftermath at the Vivekanand International Foundation, Chauhan said Indian loitering missions sent to search for radars around Sargodha ran out of fuel and ended up hitting Kirana Hills -- a site associated with Pakistan's nuclear facilities."At occasions, it's been asked whether Kirana Hills were hit or not, which is where their (Pakistan's) nuclear facilities are... Before those strikes, we had sent in a lot of loitering missions at Sargodha and Kirana Hills is about 10 kilometers north of Sargodha," Chauhan said."So the loitering mission is looking for radars which are in and around Sargodha, and it has a lifetime, which means it will loiter for about 2 hours and once it does not find a target, it comes down and hits somewhere. It must have come and hit one of those hills. So that could be one of the reasons as to what people asked, because Pakistani media also showed some kind of images in which there was smoke coming out from Kirana Hills," he added.Chauhan also revealed details of another episode during the operation, saying the Air Chief sought his approval to strike Sargodha after Pakistan requested talks. However the target was changed to Bholari due to bad weather."Once the Pakistanis had picked up the phone and said they wanted to talk at about 10 AM. The Air Chief asked me whether he should strike Sargodha, I said, Go ahead. I said, could you please identify two more targets, so one of the targets he identified was Skardu," Chauhan said."We gave a yes, but after some time, the weather was bad over it and they had to change over to Bholari," he added.During his address, Chauhan also stressed that military decisions involve varying levels of risk and must be assessed against the political objectives they are intended to achieve."Each option has a certain kind of risk involved in it, and also it will satisfy the political need for which it was to be used. So, itâs an interplay between risk and attainment of political objectives," he said.Chauhan said the operation remains relevant nearly 15 months after its major active phase ended. He said its assessment should take into account deficiencies identified during the operation, measures taken to address them and the changing nature of warfare.He added that these factors, along with wider global uncertainties, are creating new challenges for military planners.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Target apologises for 'offensive' children Halloween costume after backlash
articles.summary: The retailer says the costume is "hurtful for Black guests, team members and partners", without providing further details.
articles.body:
American retail giant Target has withdrawn a Halloween costume from sale after critics on social media said it resembled a racist caricature.

Describing the costume as "offensive", the store said in a statement that it was "hurtful for our Black guests, team members and partners", without providing further details.

Images circulating online show a costume sold as the "Kids' Glows Under Blacklight Circus Clown Halloween Costume", and customers and others on social media say it evokes blackface and minstrel shows.

"As a company, we know we got this wrong, and we are deeply sorry," Target said. "The costume is offensive and should never have been part of our assortment."

"Removing the costume is an important first step, and the company is looking closely at how this happened and what needs to change to ensure this won't happen again," Target said.

The BBC asked Target about the costume in question, but the retailer declined to comment further.

Target has recently faced supply shortages and backlash over its decision to end its diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) targets.

The company was also criticised over its handling of products in its Pride Collection in 2023.

The store is known for its affordable clothing and a wide range of groceries, household goods, electronics and toys.

articles.title: Air Force officer who died in Alaska plane crash remembered as 'positive leader'
articles.summary: The Air Force identified 2nd Lt. Leah Borsich, 23, as a victim of the deadly Alaska charter plane crash that killed all eight on board near Cape Newenham.
articles.body: A 23-year-old Air Force officer killed alongside seven others in a charter plane crash in remote western Alaska last week is being remembered as a "positive leader" who served with "professionalism, compassion and purpose." The Air Force identified 2nd Lt. Leah R. Borsich on Monday as one of the victims of the Aug. 20 crash near the Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site Airport, about 450 miles west-southwest of Anchorage. Borsich was a project programmer with the 611th Civil Engineer Squadron at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson. "Lt. Borsich was a positive leader who brought tremendous energy and enthusiasm to our command," Col. Timothey Meerstein, commander of the Pacific Air Forces Regional Support Center, said in a statement. TWO US ARMY CORPS OF ENGINEERS EMPLOYEES AMONG 8 KILLED IN ALASKA CHARTER PLANE CRASH "She led with professionalism, compassion and purpose, and her presence strengthened the bonds between the people around her," Meerstein said. "She made a lasting impact on our team, and we are grateful for her service and commitment to our nation." The Cessna 441 was carrying two pilots and six passengers when it crashed west of Cape Newenham at about 12:15 p.m. Thursday. All eight people aboard were killed. The charter plane had taken off from Ted Stevens Anchorage International Airport and was headed to Cape Newenham when it crashed during its second approach to the gravel runway in heavy fog, according to federal officials. The pilots could not see the runway and were flying by instruments, Clint Johnson, the National Transportation Safety Board’s Alaska region chief, said Friday. They aborted their first landing attempt because of poor visibility before crashing on the second approach. An observation system near the airport reported fog and visibility of about 10 miles shortly before the crash. About 15 minutes later, visibility had fallen to less than a quarter-mile, according to the National Weather Service. Search teams later found fragmented wreckage from the twin-engine plane, also known as a Cessna Conquest. The Air Force said an Army member, contractors and crew members with Anchorage-based airplane charter company Security Aviation were also among those killed. "We also mourn the loss of our Army and contractor teammates and extend our deepest appreciation to the Security Aviation aircrew, whose professionalism and dedication are vital to our mission," Meerstein said. "Their service and sacrifice will not be forgotten." Security Aviation, which operated the flight, said it was "heartbroken" by the crash. "Our hearts go out to the families, friends and loved ones of those who were lost," the company said in a statement posted to Facebook. "We extend our deepest condolences to them and to everyone affected by this devastating tragedy." Security Aviation thanked the military, Alaska Rescue Coordination Center and search-and-recovery teams that responded after the crash. The company said it is cooperating with the investigation and would not speculate about the cause. "Our focus at this time is on those who are grieving and on supporting our employees and others affected by this tremendous loss," the company said. In addition to the pilots, those aboard included two U.S. Army Corps of Engineers employees and four contractors. Two of the contractors worked for Calista Brice, which provides construction, engineering, logistics and other services in remote areas. ARMY IDENTIFIES 2 PILOTS KILLED IN APACHE HELICOPTER CRASH NEAR FORT HOOD DURING TRAINING EXERCISE The Army Corps said its employees were part of a "project delivery team en route to a project site in support of the U.S. Air Force." Officials have not said what work the group was traveling to perform. Cape Newenham is part of a network of remote radar sites that monitors aircraft operating in Alaska’s airspace and along its borders. The site, built in the 1950s as part of an early-warning network against a potential Soviet attack, now monitors the skies off Alaska’s coast in the direction of Russia, North Korea and China. Borsich’s name was released after her family had been notified. The Alaska State Troopers will release the names of the victims who were not affiliated with the Department of War, the Air Force said. Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, who leads Alaskan Command, the Alaskan North American Aerospace Defense Command Region and Eleventh Air Force, previously described those aboard as "dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment." "This is a devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve," Davis said after the crash. articles.title: CIA chief travels to Moscow for unannounced talks, US media reports
articles.summary: Flight tracking data confirms an American military aircraft travelled to Russia from the US via Latvia on Tuesday.
articles.body:
The head of the US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has travelled to Moscow for unannounced talks, the BBC's US news partner CBS has reported.

John Ratcliffe reportedly arrived in the Russian capital earlier on Tuesday. Neither Washington or Moscow have confirmed the nature of the visit or who he was due to meet.

In-person talks between high-level American and Russian officials are rare.

Flight tracking data confirmed a large US military aircraft travelled to Russia from the US via Latvia on Tuesday. It departed later on Tuesday.

BBC News has contacted the CIA, the White House and Pentagon for comment.

Footage posted on social media showed the C-17 transport plane approaching Moscow's Vnukovo international airport.

It departed Riga airport at 05:50 GMT and appeared to have landed in the Russian capital at around 07:04 GMT, according to data from FlightRadar24. It returned to Riga shortly before 17:00 GMT.

Footage on social media also purported to show a diplomatic motorcade travelling through Moscow.

Ahead of the trip, the US told Ukraine that a senior delegation would be travelling to Moscow and asked Kyiv to suspend strikes until they had left, a senior Ukrainian official told CBS.

The trip is thought to be Ratcliffe's first trip to Russia as CIA director, although he has maintained contact with his intelligence counterparts in Moscow.

John Foreman, who served as a British military attachÃ© to Moscow between 2019 and 2022, told Radio 4's PM programme that the visit could be focused on "escalation management" given speculation recent drone activity in Germany could be linked to Russia .

He said: "The Americans don't normally send such a high ranking official to Moscow unannounced at short notice unless something is up."

Foreman said the trip could also concern the release of US detainees currently being held in Russia.

Ratcliffe played a role in negotiations for the release of Russian-American citizen Ksenia Karelina, who was jailed in Russia for over a year after being accused of providing support to Ukraine.

The CIA was also involved in a 2024 prisoner swap deal with Russia that saw the release of Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich, as well as former US marine Paul Whelan and Russian-American journalist Alsu Kurmasheva.

The US has had strained relations with Russia since it launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, Russia has been isolated on the world stage and faced international economic sanctions.

Ratcliffe appears to be one of the highest-ranking US officials to visit the country during President Donald Trump's second term.

Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin at a summit in Alaska last year but the meeting did not lead to a breakthrough. Subsequent US-led peace talks between Russia and Ukraine appear to have stalled.

Additional reporting by Washington correspondent Daniel Bush and BBC Verify

Footage posted on social media showed the C-17 transport plane approaching Moscow's Vnukovo international airport.

The US has had strained relations with Russia since it launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Since then, Russia has been isolated on the world stage and faced international economic sanctions.

Ratcliffe appears to be one of the highest-ranking US officials to visit the country during President Donald Trump's second term.

Trump met Russian President Vladimir Putin at a summit in Alaska last year but the meeting did not lead to a breakthrough. Subsequent US-led peace talks between Russia and Ukraine appear to have stalled.

articles.title: Archaeologists found a 7,000-year-old pit packed with beaver bones; it reveals how Europe's first farmers used animal fur
articles.summary: Europe News: Archaeologists in Germany have uncovered a Stone Age pit near Alsleben, Saxony-Anhalt, containing the bones of at least twelve beavers, offering an un.
articles.body: Archaeologists in Germany have uncovered a Stone Age pit near Alsleben, Saxony-Anhalt, containing the bones of at least twelve beavers, offering an unusually vivid window into how Europe's earliest farmers exploited animal fur. The roughly 7,000-year-old feature was first unearthed in 2024 during surveys ahead of construction of the SuedOstLink power line, and has now been dated to between 4935 and 4787 BC, placing it within the Linear Pottery culture.The bones, described by researchers as "exceptionally well preserved and mostly unfragmented," show no anatomical connection to one another, suggesting the beavers were skinned and their carcasses left to decompose before the remains were finally gathered and buried together. Excavated by the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology (LDA) of Saxony-Anhalt, the find points to a deliberate, organised hunting episode, and hints at the surprisingly elaborate fur clothing worn by some of the continent's first farming communities.7,000-year-old beaver bones found along a major power line routeThe find emerged during preparatory archaeological surveys for the SuedOstLink, a major high-voltage direct current power line being built across Saxony-Anhalt. Investigations in the Salzland district were carried out by the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology (LDA) of Saxony-Anhalt, working closely with grid operator 50Hertz ahead of construction work along the route.The power line stretches roughly 170 kilometres through the state, running largely alongside the A14 and A9 motorways and cutting through what the LDA describes as old settlement land with exceptionally fertile soils. This has meant an unusually high concentration of archaeological sites requiring excavation and documentation before building work can proceed, and it was this process that first brought the pit to light near Alsleben in 2024.How archaeologists found a beaver bone pit near the Saale RiverThe site itself sits above the Saale River, at the point where the power line is due to cross beneath it using a trenchless tunnelling method. According to the press release by the State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology Saxony-Anhalt, the area "had already been chosen as a settlement site in the Neolithic period (New Stone Age) and was also used during the Bronze and Iron Ages," making it a long-favoured spot for human occupation across millennia.Amid a dense scatter of postholes, storage pits and burial sites, one feature caught researchers' attention. Archaeologists describe an "initially inconspicuous-looking pit, approximately 80 centimetres in diameter," which turned out to be tightly packed with animal bone. The distinctive orange-to-reddish-brown teeth scattered through the fill immediately identified the remains as beaver. A flint tool found near the surface of the deposit hinted at an early date, prompting the team to lift the entire feature as a soil block for careful excavation under laboratory conditions.Why the 7,000-year-old beaver pit belonged to the Linear Pottery cultureRadiocarbon analysis has since pinned the pit firmly to between 4935 and 4787 BC, placing it within the Linear Pottery culture, one of the earliest farming societies to spread across central Europe. Crucially, the bone assemblage is unusually pure: it consists exclusively of beaver remains, and the bones themselves are described as "exceptionally well preserved and mostly unfragmented."Skull evidence points to a minimum of twelve individual beavers, spanning a wide range of ages from under a year old to more than eight years. Yet the bones show no anatomical connection to one another, and several elements are missing altogether, strong evidence, researchers say, that the carcasses were already fully skeletonised by the time they were finally buried in the pit.How the beaver bones reveal a deliberate hunting and fur-making processTaken together, the evidence points to a single, deliberate hunting episode rather than gradual accumulation over time. The LDA suggests the beavers were hunted along the Saale, skinned for their pelts, and their carcasses then left to decompose elsewhere before the disarticulated bones were finally gathered and disposed of in the pit, a two-stage process that speaks to a surprisingly organised approach to fur production.For researchers, the implications go well beyond hunting technique. As the LDA notes, the find "not only points to specialised hunting strategies in the early Neolithic period, but also allows us to draw conclusions about the clothing worn during this time, which we can imagine to have been quite elaborate." It is a rare direct link between a single archaeological deposit and the everyday material culture, in this case, warm, durable fur garments, of some of Europe's earliest farming communities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: A New Jersey artist bought a 600-square-foot cabin in 1989 and kept adding to it; 37 years later, Luna Parc is a 5,000-square-foot home, studio and living artwork still being built
articles.summary: US News: When Ricky Boscarino came across a small 600-square-foot cabin in the woods in New Jersey in 1988, he saw more than just a place to live. A year later.
articles.body: When Ricky Boscarino came across a small 600-square-foot cabin in the woods in New Jersey in 1988, he saw more than just a place to live. A year later, he began transforming it into what would become his largest work in progress called Luna Parc.More than three decades later, the property in Sandyston Township has grown into a 5,000-square-foot home, studio and working art environment. According to SPACES Archives, the property now has 11 levels and 15 rooms, with each part reflecting Boscarino's work as an artist and craftsman.Boscarino, also known as Ricky of Luna Parc, comes from an artistic family. His family history, according to the Luna Parc website, goes back to the time of the Medici. He has continued that connection through his own work in metal, clay, glass, wood and cement.He graduated from the Rhode Island School of Design in 1982. His interest in creating unusual and detailed objects had developed much earlier. As a young student, he was recognised for making carefully crafted dioramas, including scenes of cockroaches in beauty salons and nativity scenes.Cabin became life-sized artworkBoscarino started transforming the New Jersey cabin in 1989. What began as a 600-square-foot structure eventually became a much larger space that combines his home and atelier.SPACES Archives describes Luna Parc as a personal home, working studio, living classroom and community artist space. The property has continued to develop as Boscarino has added new elements and used different materials and objects throughout the site.The entrance itself reflects this approach. A ferrocement structure welcomes visitors to the property and has been named the 'Artichoke Portico' by Boscarino.Inside, the rooms have their own themes and collections. The kitchen, for example, is decorated with milk tabs and nearly 20,000 wine corks placed along the walls. Other spaces include the Hall of Hats, Nature Lab, a weaving studio, a mosaiced bathroom and the Asia Room.The Asia Room contains a set of doors that are almost 200 years old. These objects are part of the wider collection that Boscarino has built into the property over the years.Objects from around the worldBoscarino is both an artist and a collector. He has travelled to more than 40 countries and brought back a practice or item from each place, incorporating them into Luna Parc.One of the spaces inside the home is the Ballroom. It contains Morse code messages, a real human skeleton and painted portraits created by Boscarino.The Ballroom is used to host artists and students for lectures and readings about different ways of working as an artist.As the house rises upwards, the spaces continue to change. Boscarino's bedroom is on the seventh level. At the top is the Sky Walk, decorated with whirlygigs and kinetic sculptures.From the Sky Walk, there is a view across the property and the garden. The outdoor area includes a cobalt blue bottle house and a garden designed to light up at night.There is also a small purple chapel on the property. It is surrounded by a fence made from crutches that Boscarino created in honour of his grandfather.The Chapel of the Saints and the crutch fence commemorate an event that Boscarino's grandfather witnessed as a child. According to the SPACES account, his grandfather saw a young man regain the ability to walk in front of him.Young artists learn at Luna ParcThe property is not only Boscarino's home and studio. Beyond the garden and chapel is his Atelier, where he works with interns who are young local artists.The programme gives them an opportunity to learn his techniques and craft. It also aims to show them another way of living and working as an artist.This part of Luna Parc became more formally organised in 2015, when Boscarino established the Luna Parc Atelier Foundation Inc. The foundation is an official non-profit.The foundation's programme also focuses on helping apprentices develop practical skills. According to the Luna Parc website, it âteaches apprentices hand working and business skills necessary to succeed as self-supporting artists,â while also caring for the home and its future.Luna Parc is not generally open to the public for tours. SPACES notes that visits are limited to certain Open House days.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Trump says all mines cleared from Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Iran has closed the vital waterway since the beginning of the conflict causing wild fluctuations in oil prices worldwide.
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said that the US Navy has removed or detonated all mines in the Strait of Hormuz - the vital waterway which Iran has largely closed since the beginning of the war in the Middle East.

"Iran has been notified that any ship or boat placing new mines will be immediately and systematically destroyed," Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform.

Closure of the strait has caused wild fluctuations in the price of oil on world markets. Trump has often said the US has control of the area - but Iran has fired against vessels it says have sought to cross without its permission.

Some 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas used to transit the Strait of Hormuz before the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli air strikes against Iran.

In addition to closing the strait, Iran retaliated against Israel and against US bases in the region as well as US Arab allies in the Gulf.

A ceasefire aimed at facilitating talks to end the war has collapsed and there has been intermittent exchange of fire between the US and Iran.

However, this week the US announced a raft of economic sanctions against Iran.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned that any nation financially partnering with Iran would be isolated.

Iran and the US signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in June - a 14-point document which set a 60-day deadline to reach a deal on the Strait of Hormuz, before substantial negotiations on resolving the nuclear issue - allegations that Iran is building a nuclear weapon, which Tehran has consistently denied.

However, that deadline has now expired and talks have collapsed leading to the new US sanctions that Trump believes will lead to the collapse of the Iranian regime.

Iran has been under sanctions for most of the time since the founding of the Islamic Republic in 1979 and Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh said Tehran was "fully prepared" for the wider sanctions, which he added would lead to "another defeat" for the US.

Its economy, however, has suffered as a result of the war - and a blockade of Iranian ports that the US has been maintaining for weeks not to allow trade to continue.

On Tuesday, China - the biggest buyer of Iranian oil - said it was firmly opposed to what it called the US's "illegal unilateral sanctions" and would take "all necessary measures" to safeguard its rights.

The US announcement comes ahead of planned talks between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping next month.

Washington is likely to be wary of potential retaliation from Beijing, which processes the majority of the world's rare earths and other critical minerals, crucial in the manufacture of many high-tech products.

Beijing has already tightened export controls on rare earths as part of previous trade negotiations with the US.

Iran, for its part, has indicated that it wants to establish full control of the Strait of Hormuz - a view that is opposed by the US and most other countries which believe that the passage constitutes international waters and transit should remain unimpeded as it was before the war.

Until recently - and on the basis of the MoU - Iran had been involved in negotiations with Oman, a US ally, to agree a mechanism for administering the strait. However, those talks have so far not produced an agreement and, last week, Trump even threatened to bomb its ally "if it gets in the way" of his administration's own talks with Iran over the issue.

Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi said on Tuesday that he hoped his country and Iran would soon announce the establishment of a temporary shipping corridor in the strait after meeting his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Tehran.

He said in a statement he also hoped for "practical arrangements" to restore safe navigation, adding: "Future management of the strait and a permanent solution will follow in due course."

Araghchi confirmed the meeting in a statement, saying "regional solutions" were discussed in talks with representatives from Pakistan and Oman.

He added that discussions covered the future management of the strait, as well as the framework for a new corridor and a joint mine-clearing operation.

Speaking to state television news after the meeting Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabad said the entry route to the Gulf would be "through Iranian waters and the exit route through Omani territorial waters, and ships will pass through Iranian waters on both routes".

The minister added that the south corridor of the waterway, which has been recommended to shipping firms by the US and is situated close to the coast of Oman , would be "closed" under the framework, and the meeting "does not mean that the Strait will be opened from tomorrow".

He said "no military vessels will be allowed to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, and only commercial vessels will be allowed to pass through it".

Gharibabad called the route "temporary", adding Iran and Oman will negotiate a new permanent route within a timeframe of 60 days to replace the previous maritime traffic plan.

"If Iran's requests are not granted, the Strait will be closed," he said.

articles.title: SNAP rolls are shrinking fast. This map shows which states have seen the biggest drops.
articles.summary: Nearly 5.6 million fewer people are receiving food assistance than a year ago, with some states seeing much steeper declines.
articles.body:
The number of people receiving food assistance through the nation's largest federal food aid program has fallen by more than 5 million over the past year.

Participation in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) has decreased by more than 13% as stricter eligibility rules and work requirements take effect. The biggest declines have been seen in the South and Southwest of the country.

Data released by the USDA this month showed SNAP enrollment provisionally fell to 36.6 million in May 2026 from 42.2 million in May 2025. This provisional figure would make the number of people receiving SNAP as low as it was forecast to reach in 2030, according to the Associated Press.

The decline comes as changes to SNAP have expanded work requirements and tightened eligibility rules as part of President Trump's One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA).

The changes mean more people must now work, volunteer or take part in job training for at least 80 hours a month to continue receiving SNAP, or risk losing benefits. This rule was extended to include adults up to age 64 and parents of children 14 and older. The law also removed automatic exemptions for veterans, people experiencing homelessness and former foster youth. Exemptions remain for those 65 and older, parents of children younger than 14, and people with disabilities or health limitations.

Some states have seen sharper drops than others, which you can see in the map below.

In Arizona, the number of people receiving SNAP fell by 53.8% from May 2025 to May 2026, while Georgia saw a 36.5% decline over the same period, according to USDA's figures .

Arizona officials said the drop was driven largely by the state's struggles to put the new federal requirements in place.

"Implementing the federally mandated changes triggered unprecedented call volumes and administrative hurdles, including additional verification requirements, creating real barriers for applicants," Brett Bezio, a spokesman for the Arizona Department of Economic Security, told the Associated Press .

Bezio said hiring more staff members and introducing ways for people to submit documents online have helped stem the decline in participation in recent months and reduced the risk that eligible people will lose benefits.

Supporters of the changes introduced by the OBBBA argue that tighter eligibility rules will reduce improper payments and encourage more adults to work.

In an article looking into the fall in SNAP participants last week, the Cato Institute said: "Much of SNAP's enrollment decline reflects states unwinding pandemic-era waivers and eligibility rules that kept caseloads elevated."

It added, "Judge the success of OBBBA's SNAP reforms, and all welfare programs, by how many people move out of welfare and into self-sufficiency, not by how many are kept on it."

Grocery prices in U.S. cities have risen 33% since the beginning of 2019, according to government figures. By comparison, they rose just 6.4% over the previous seven-and-a-half years.

In Florida, where SNAP participation fell 22% in the year to May 2026, Paco Velez, president and CEO of Feeding South Florida, said part of the decline may be driven by immigrants who are in the U.S. legally but fear being targeted by the Trump administration's immigration crackdown if they seek government benefits.

Critics of the SNAP reforms say the new requirements create administrative hurdles that can cause eligible people to lose food assistance.

Some food banks have increased food distributions to try to meet demand that they say has risen as SNAP participation has declined. But advocates say they cannot fully make up the difference.

Reflecting on the changes to SNAP earlier this month, nonprofit No Kid Hungry said: "Already 4.5 million people, including over a million kids, have lost access to SNAP over the past year. Those families are now missing out on the nutritious food SNAP provides, and sadly that number will only grow."

The decline may not be over. Starting in October 2027, states will have to pay a share of SNAP benefit costs if their payment error rates exceed 6% — a change advocates warn could push states to tighten eligibility further to avoid the added expense, potentially creating new barriers for recipients in the years ahead.

articles.summary: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s interventions in the U.S.-Canada trade talks helped the weeks-long negotiations fall apart, according to multiple reports, thrusting the two countries into a trade war. U.S. and Canadian officials had felt good about an outline of a trade deal struck last Tuesday ahead of the original Wednesday deadline. President Trump took to…
articles.body:
Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s interventions in the U.S.-Canada trade talks helped the weeks-long negotiations fall apart, according to multiple reports, thrusting the two countries into a trade war .

U.S. and Canadian officials had felt good about an outline of a trade deal struck last Tuesday ahead of the original Wednesday deadline. President Trump took to social media to say that a deal had been struck, and he was pausing the 50 percent tariffs on some Canadian goods until Friday to finalize the paperwork.

But Lutnick was leery of Canadian proposals that would lower the tariff on autos to a level lower than what he wanted, according to The New York Times . He said instead that only a certain volume of aluminum should get lower tariff rates, and that heavy trucks should not have tariffs lowered like cars.

Canada produces some heavy trucks at the General Motors and Ford plants in Ontario.

Canadians put the blame on Lutnick for moving the goalposts at the eleventh hour, according to Bloomberg , while some business leaders were happy he was making demands on a deal they saw as hurting the U.S. metals industries.

When asked Saturday whether Lutnick’s involvement in the final days of negotiations was an impediment, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said that’s “a question for the U.S. administration.”

Carney said his Canadian team was “unified … but you cannot say that about the United States administration.”

The talks between the U.S. and Canada fell apart on Friday, just hours before the tariffs were set to go into effect on items including wine, hockey sticks, cement and others.

Canada vowed to “match those tariffs dollar for dollar.” The tariffs apply to around $20 billion of Canadian goods.

Since then, Trump has threatened further hits on Canada — in the form of 50 percent tariffs on cars, trucks, auto parts and steel that would go into effect on New Year’s Day.

He accused Canada of “ripping off the United States of America for years” in a Truth Social post.

“On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with,” he wrote. “They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US! They do 95% of their business with the U.S., with us, the exact opposite!”

Canada said Monday it is expected to unveil retaliatory tariffs on the U.S. on Tuesday. They would go into effect on Sept. 8.

articles.title: Indiana power outages: Gov. Braun demands NIPSCO investigation as Gary residents hit day 13
articles.summary: State officials want the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission to investigate how NIPSCO customers’ dollars were spent.
articles.body: After nearly two weeks without power for thousands of people across northwest Indiana, Gov. Mike Braun is calling for an investigation into NIPSCO. “NIPSCO is a monopoly utility that Hoosiers pay every month with the expectation that it will use its considerable resources to maintain its system, prepare for severe weather and restore service as quickly as possible when disaster strikes,” Braun said in a news release. “NIPSCO has failed to keep its end of the bargain.” Braun is calling for a thorough review of NIPSCO’s preparation for and response to the recent power outages. On Monday, he directed the Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor to file a complaint and petition the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission to launch an investigation into NIPSCO. The governor said the crews on the ground did an extraordinary job but “NIPSCO management has failed to deliver adequate solutions.” In response, NIPSCO said it will continue to communicate with Braun’s administration. “NIPSCO values the regulatory process and will cooperate fully if the Commission were to open an investigation. We are committed to transparency and cooperation in providing information regarding our operations and ongoing efforts to serve our customers safely and reliably,” the company said in a statement. There are streets all over the region, including in Hammond, Munster and Gary, where people still don’t have power. Every day, Andre Abrams hopes today will be the day power returns to his neighborhood in Gary. “It’s been a lot of stress,” Abrams said. “It’s Day 13 now. Tomorrow [is Day] 14.” Two weeks without electricity has forced his family to find new ways to get by, including using a lighter to light up the stove in order to cook. “Four workers went to the back to check out the transformer yesterday but ... we need a whole new pole,” said Makinna Cain. The good news is NBC Chicago did see NIPSCO, contracted linemen and ComEd on the ground in Gary. “Without lights, we’re worried about staying here in the dark, but we don’t want to leave our house because somebody might break in it. Then that leaves us with more problems,” said Jamesetta White, who lives in Gary. “I know they’re probably doing the best they can do. I don’t want to put anyone down. I just pray to God that they hurry up.” NIPSCO said it’s “committed to restoring power safely and as quickly as possible for every customer affected by this historic storm.” Families across the area said they’ve had to throw out food. There are health concerns, too. “I have a heart monitor and once the electricity has been off this long, the hospital, the doctors cannot monitor that monitor because it’s off. So, hopefully nothing has happened to me yet,” said Rutha Taylor, who lives in Gary. State officials are asking the commission to investigate how NIPSCO customers’ dollars were spent, including more than $81 million meant for vegetation management from 2023 to 2025 and $2.3 billion meant to replace aging infrastructure since 2016, according to a spokesperson for the Indiana Office of Utility Consumer Counselor. “Since we lost our food and have been out with our lights, I think they should not have us to pay a bill for a whole month. That would give us [time to] catch up,” White said.

articles.title: El coche nuevo más barato de mantener en Estados Unidos es uno que casi nadie compra
articles.summary: El Fiat 500e lidera un estudio como el coche nuevo más barato de mantener en EE. UU., mientras híbridos y eléctricos muestran importantes diferencias en cost...
articles.body:
Comprar un coche y mantenerlo durante años son dos cuestiones muy diferentes. Un estudio de Self.Inc que analiza 50 modelos nuevos vendidos en Estados Unidos ha dejado un resultado tan curioso como inesperado: el Fiat 500e es el coche nuevo más barato de mantener del mercado, con un coste medio anual de apenas 3.557 dólares.

El dato resulta todavía más llamativo si tenemos en cuenta que el pequeño eléctrico italiano prácticamente ha desaparecido de las calles estadounidenses: Fiat vendió solamente 150 unidades durante la primera mitad del año, un 81% menos que en el mismo periodo de 2025.

El Fiat 500e gana gracias a unos costes sorprendentemente bajos

El secreto del Fiat 500e está principalmente en su reducido tamaño, su mecánica eléctrica y unos gastos contenidos en prácticamente todas las categorías analizadas.

Su coste energético anual se sitúa en 779 dólares, exactamente la misma cantidad estimada para el seguro, mientras que el mantenimiento representa otros 1.275 dólares. Los impuestos y tasas suman 724 dólares.

En conjunto, el modelo italiano se distancia claramente del segundo clasificado, el Honda Civic Hybrid , que alcanza 4.833 dólares anuales. Tras ellos aparecen el Hyundai Elantra , con 4.904 dólares; el Nissan Versa , con 4.949; y el Toyota Camry Hybrid , con 5.031 dólares.

La clasificación también deja una conclusión interesante para quienes están pensando en electrificarse. Aunque pueda parecer lógico que un eléctrico sea siempre más económico de mantener, el estudio señala que los vehículos híbridos presentan un coste medio anual de 5.734 dólares, frente a los 6.189 dólares de los eléctricos.

Los coches de gasolina son los más costosos de media, con 7.025 dólares anuales.

Entre los 20 modelos más económicos también aparecen el Honda Accord Hybrid, Honda Civic, MINI Cooper, Kia K4, Mazda3, Dodge Charger Daytona, Tesla Model 3 y Hyundai Ioniq 6, demostrando que existen alternativas muy diferentes para quienes buscan reducir el coste de propiedad.

En el extremo contrario aparece uno de los deportivos más reconocidos del mundo. El Porsche 911 encabeza la lista de los coches nuevos más caros de mantener, con un coste medio anual de nada menos que 10.832 dólares.

El modelo alemán está seguido por el Audi RS7 , con 10.334 dólares; el Cadillac CT5-V Blackwing , con 10.265; el Chevrolet Corvette , con 10.213; y el eléctrico Lucid Air , con 10.049 dólares. En este último caso, el reducido gasto energético no evita que el seguro y otros costes eleven considerablemente la factura anual.

La evolución respecto al estudio anterior también resulta significativa. El gasto medio anual en combustible ha descendido de 2.246 a 1.727 dólares, pero esa mejora ha quedado parcialmente neutralizada por el incremento del seguro, que pasó de 1.763 a 2.219 dólares, y del mantenimiento, que aumentó desde 1.633 hasta 1.817 dólares. Además, los impuestos y tasas también han subido.

Por eso, al comprar un vehículo nuevo no basta con mirar el precio de adquisición o el consumo homologado: seguro, mantenimiento, impuestos y energía pueden cambiar por completo la cuenta final.

Entre los modelos más interesantes por equilibrio aparecen el Nissan Versa, Toyota Camry Hybrid, Honda Accord Hybrid y Mazda3, mientras que incluso propuestas deportivas como el Hyundai Elantra N consiguen sorprender por sus costes relativamente contenidos.

El estudio, eso sí, debe interpretarse como una referencia y no como una garantía de gasto individual, ya que el precio del seguro, los kilómetros recorridos, el estado del vehículo y los costes locales pueden modificar notablemente la factura de cada propietario.

Aun así, el dato del Fiat 500e deja una conclusión difícil de ignorar: el coche que menos cuesta mantener en Estados Unidos es precisamente uno de los que menos éxito comercial está teniendo.

articles.title: Mentmore Towers, Batman Beginsâ Wayne Manor in Buckinghamshire, could be seized as owners face deadline to repair crumbling mansion and conduct bat surveys to save historic property
articles.summary: UK News: The real-life Wayne Manor from Christopher Nolanâs Batman Begins, Mentmore Towers in Buckinghamshire, is at the centre of a preservation battle after .
articles.body: The real-life Wayne Manor from Christopher Nolanâs Batman Begins, Mentmore Towers in Buckinghamshire, is at the centre of a preservation battle after the Grade I-listed mansion was served with a formal repairs notice. The property could ultimately face a compulsory purchase order if its owners fail to take action, while authorities have also required specialist bat surveys before restoration work can proceed.Mentmore Towers, the sprawling country house that doubled as Bruce Wayneâs iconic home in Batman Begins, has been described as being in âvery badâ condition by Historic England. Buckinghamshire Council has now issued a listed-building repairs notice, saying the work is âreasonably necessary for the proper preservationâ of the historic property.The notice comes amid concerns over the deterioration of the mansion, including its roofs, chimneys, rooflights, roof lanterns and leadwork. Photographs included in the notice reportedly show cracks in walls, broken windows and ivy-covered walls. During a visit to the property, officials also found evidence of bats, according to SWNS.Batmanâs Wayne Manor faces a preservation battleMentmore Towers was built between 1852 and 1854 for the Rothschild family and is considered the only major surviving work of architect Sir Joseph Paxton, who also designed Londonâs Crystal Palace.The mansion later gained global pop-culture recognition when it was used as Wayne Manor in Christopher Nolanâs Batman Begins. The property has also appeared in films including The Mummy Returns, Ali G Indahouse and Johnny English.Its cinematic history, however, has not prevented growing concerns about its physical condition.Buckinghamshire Council has ordered the owners to demonstrate that they are appointing a contractor with experience in repairing listed buildings. The authorities have also required three bat-emergence surveys to be completed by August 2027, along with any necessary Natural England licence and recommendations arising from the surveys.Once repair work begins, council and Historic England officers must also be permitted to inspect the property weekly.Council warns of possible compulsory purchaseThe repairs notice represents a significant escalation in the long-running concerns surrounding Mentmore Towers.If the required action is not taken, Buckinghamshire Council could seek government approval to acquire the mansion through a compulsory purchase order, alongside pursuing further legal action.The development has been welcomed by heritage campaigners.Henrietta Billings, director of SAVE Britainâs Heritage, said the organisation welcomed Buckinghamshire Councilâs decision to require the current owner to undertake âurgent and overdue repairsâ to the historic house.âWe urge the owners, who have owned the building for over 25 years, to step up and undertake immediate repairs,â she said. âThis exceptional landmark has been neglected for too long.âWho owns the real Wayne Manor?Mentmore Towers is owned by Syrian-British businessman Simon Halabi, who purchased the property in 1999 after it had been put up for sale two years earlier.Halabi had ambitious plans for the estate, intending to transform Mentmore Towers into a luxury hotel featuring 171 suites.Those plans became embroiled in a legal battle in 2004 after local resident Jonathan Davey obtained a last-minute injunction at the High Court to stop the proposed development.A judicial review subsequently examined whether the conditions attached to the planning permission had been followed. In March 2005, the High Court ruled that the decision to grant planning permission was âunimpeachableâ.However, the proposed luxury hotel never became a reality. Halabiâs property company later ran into financial difficulties amid the collapse of the housing market, and the hotel plans were abandoned.From Rothschild mansion to Batmanâs Wayne ManorBefore Halabi acquired the property, Mentmore Towers had already undergone several changes in its history.In 1992, the previous owners established a country club at the estate, complete with an 18-hole golf course. The club eventually ceased trading in 2015.More recently, company documents filed with Companies House in May reportedly show that Mentmore Towers Ltd, of which Halabi is a director, is a dormant company, meaning it is not currently trading or generating other income such as investments.Despite the uncertainty surrounding its future, Mentmore Towers remains one of Britainâs most recognisable historic estates.Mentmore Towersâ Hollywood historyFor Batman fans, the property is best known as Wayne Manor in Batman Begins, where it provided the exterior setting for Bruce Wayneâs ancestral home.But its screen history extends well beyond Gotham.Mentmore Towers has featured in The Mummy Returns, Ali G Indahouse and Johnny English, while its grand interiors and distinctive architecture have also appeared in music videos.The mansion was used in Haddawayâs âWhat Is Loveâ music video and the Spice Girlsâ âGoodbyeâ video.Now, however, the historic building faces a very real battle far removed from the fictional world of Batman. Unless the necessary repairs, ecological surveys and preservation measures are carried out, the future of the real-life Wayne Manor could ultimately be decided by the authorities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Canada announces ‘dollar for dollar, rate for rate’ retaliatory tariffs on US
articles.summary: Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on hundreds of American products as high as 50 percent Tuesday, just days after the collapse of negotiations between the two countries. Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Canada will match the U.S.’s tariffs “dollar for dollar, rate for rate.” The tariffs would take effect Sept. 8. He said the 15…
articles.body:
Canada announced retaliatory tariffs on hundreds of American products as high as 50 percent Tuesday, just days after the collapse of negotiations between the two countries.

Canadian Finance Minister François-Philippe Champagne said Canada will match the U.S.’s tariffs “dollar for dollar, rate for rate.” The tariffs would take effect Sept. 8.

He said the 15 percent, 25 percent and 50 percent tariffs will be on $27.6 billion of imports from the U.S.

“For each product, our tariff will match the American tariff on the same type of Canadian good,” he said.

Arguably the biggest measure is Canada doubling its tariffs on U.S. steel and aluminum to 50 percent to match the 50 percent the U.S. put on Canadian steel and aluminum.

“Those tariffs will have real consequences for Canadian workers, businesses, and communities across our nation,” Champagne said of the U.S. tariffs. “Canada must respond, and today we are in a proportionate, targeted, and strategic way.”

He said the countertariffs “are designed primarily to provide protection for Canadian industries impacted by the U.S. tariffs and allow them to compete against U.S. products in the Canadian market.”

Canada released a list of over 700 items that will be targeted with tariffs ranging from live fish, frozen fish, cheese, some apparel, carpets and metal products made of steel or aluminum, among others.

The U.S.’s 50 percent tariffs went into effect on Saturday across over $20 billion of Canadian imports after negotiations collapsed late Friday.

Trump threatened to impose 50 percent tariffs on a plethora of Canadian imports in response to “discriminatory” trade measures. The U.S. tariffs fall under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, the administration said when announcing them last month.

Section 338 is a long-dormant law that allows the president to impose tariffs of up to 50 percent on a country found to discriminate against U.S. products. It does not require an investigation before tariffs are imposed.

Trump on Monday then threatened to hit Canada with 50 percent tariffs on imported cars, trucks, auto parts and steel, which would take effect on New Year’s Day.

“Canada has been ripping off the United States of America for years,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Their ridiculously high tariffs on our Farmers and farm products has made life impossible for these great American Patriots, and has long created a 60 Billion Dollar Deficit between our two Countries. Not sustainable, and NOT ANYMORE!”

Trump said Canada will no longer “be treated like a State.”

“On Trade, and in other ways, also, they are among the worst Nations in the World to deal with,” he said. “They feel entitled, and yet, WE DON’T NEED CANADA, THEY NEED US! They do 95% of their business with the U.S., with us, the exact opposite!”

Canada for its part has remained strong against the U.S. measures. Canadian officials also announced a $7.5 billion CAD package to help support domestic businesses that are harmed by the tariffs.

articles.title: Nevada wildfire contained to 27 percent as thousands still displaced
articles.summary: The third wildfire in two weeks devastates neighbourhoods across Reno, home to major entertainment and casino resorts.
articles.body:
Fire containment has reached 27 percent in the rampant wildfire that first erupted in the Sierra Nevada foothills near the city of Reno in the state of Nevada in the United States. At least seven people – three first responders and four civilians – have been injured.

The blaze first broke out on Saturday and exploded in size by Sunday, destroying at least 32 homes and damaging six as it spread perilously close to dense neighbourhoods. Local officials, speaking at an afternoon news briefing on Monday, said those numbers are sure to rise as assessment teams begin to survey the charred areas.

They also said the fire had no new growth and has held steady at about 60 square kilometres (23 square miles) since it burned out of control on Sunday.

“We are making progress,” assured US Forest Service District Ranger Matt Zumstein.

Videos posted on social media showed the smouldering ruins of homes and cars, with only a scorched basketball hoop still standing.

By Monday, the number of residents under evacuation orders and warnings was lowered to about 63,000, down from more than 90,000 people when the blaze first mushroomed over the weekend. While winds have eased, there are still concerns that gusts could propel the flames through dry brush into newly developed neighbourhoods in Nevada’s largest city outside of metro Las Vegas. Reno is home to about 280,000 people.

Schools across the local area were closed because of the evacuations and to keep roads clear for emergency crews.

‘Like nothing I’ve seen before’: Reno faces third wildfire in two weeks

Reno Mayor Hillary Schieve said the way the fire spread so quickly at its peak had her fearing for the worst.

“It lit up these areas like nothing I’ve seen before,” she said Monday, adding, “it took your breath away, in the worst way”.

This is the third large wildfire in the craggy, high-desert region north of Reno in just the past two weeks – driven completely by human behaviour, according to fire officials. They have not disclosed whether the Hawk Fire, which is what the blaze is known as due to having started near the Hawk Meadow Trail, was intentionally set or accidental. Much of the area that burned was sagebrush and grass.

Resident Crystal Hallock, 53, has lost her home to a fire twice in under a decade. She moved into the rebuilt house in 2019, a year after an electrical fire burned it down.

Nevada’s governor quickly declared a state of emergency in Washoe County over the weekend after mobilising the National Guard to help with aerial firefighting and protecting evacuated neighbourhoods northwest of downtown Reno. But at one roadblock, residents expressed frustration that they could not get back into their homes, according to The Associated Press news agency.

“There’s no fire here! Why are the National Guard here?” a driver yelled.

Washoe County Sheriff Darin Balaam said he understands that some residents are frustrated that they can’t get home, but the danger isn’t over yet. “It just takes that little breeze and one ember,” he said.

Reno is southwest of Nevada’s Black Rock Desert, site of the annual Burning Man festival, which begins on August 30.

Many who travel to Burning Man make Reno a regular pit stop. Organisers on Monday requested that attendees not take hotel rooms and other resources away from fire evacuees, while being mindful of closures.

“Treat our neighbors, first responders, hospitality workers and everyone affected by this emergency with patience and care,” a Burning Man statement read.

Much of Nevada’s western edge is under an increased risk of wildfires this week because of high winds and low relative humidity, the National Interagency Fire Center said. The National Weather Service says the region will see warm, dry and breezy conditions, and that critical fire weather conditions are possible in the week’s latter half. Reno sits at an elevation of 1,370 metres (4,500 feet).

Extremely dry conditions across the American West have sparked a rash of wildfires this summer. Fires in eastern Washington state forced the evacuation of 60,000 people in the Spokane area in early August.

Nationwide wildfires have topped 50,000 this year, marking a 10-year high for the same period, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.
