articles.title: Doug Ford responds to Trump’s Lake Ontario taunt: ‘A lot of rhetoric’
articles.summary: Ontario Premier Doug Ford dismissed President Trump’s Tuesday threat to rename a Canadian lake in honor of the U.S., a day after the pair publicly exchanged insults amid an escalating trade fight between the two countries. “I think it’s a lot of rhetoric,” Ford told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer, noting Canada’s role as a “number one…
articles.body:
Ontario Premier Doug Ford dismissed President Trump’s Tuesday threat to rename a Canadian lake in honor of the U.S., a day after the pair publicly exchanged insults amid an escalating trade fight between the two countries.

“I think it’s a lot of rhetoric,” Ford told CNN’s Wolf Blitzer, noting Canada’s role as a “number one customer” for more than a dozen U.S. states.

“We’re strong believers in being a sovereign country, and when President Trump wants to attack our sovereignty and attack our businesses and people in Ontario, I can’t roll over,” he said. “My job is to protect Ontario and Canada, and ironically, protecting the American people.”

The president wrote in a Truth Social post on Tuesday morning that his administration was “giving serious consideration” to renaming Lake Ontario to “Lake America” amid the trade war between the U.S. and Canada.

Trump added that he did not “expect to be doing much business with Ontario any longer.”

The post followed Trump’s earlier move to impose 50 percent tariffs on Canadian goods.

Ford lashed out at these levies on Monday, reiterating his threat to cut the province’s power exports to U.S. states. Ontario’s power grid directly connects to Michigan, New York and Minnesota.

“We power 1.5 million homes and businesses. Everything’s on the table. I’ll do whatever it takes,” the Canadian official told reporters.

Ford called on both sides of the fight to bring down the temperature on Tuesday, acknowledging in his interview with CNN that “things got a little heated” between him and the president.

“Let’s negotiate a fair deal because it’s hurting the U.S. It’s hurting Canada, and we just want to make sure that we have a fair deal,” he said.

Canada announced Tuesday retaliatory tariffs of up to 50 percent on a wide range of U.S. goods that will go into effect on Sept. 8. This came after Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney’s statement last week that the country would match the U.S. tariffs “dollar for dollar.”

Ford told CNN that the U.S. tariffs ultimately harm Americans.

“I do not understand why he wants to attack Canada nonstop,” he said. “We’re the closest friends and allies, and make no mistake about it, Canadians still love the American people. They love the U.S.”

articles.title: Russia’s infrastructure is being pummeled by Ukrainian strikes. Now Putin wants to seize control of it
articles.summary: Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree giving the government powers to temporarily take control of “critical infrastructure” across the country, if private owners fail to protect it from escalating Ukrainian attacks.
articles.body: Russian President Vladimir Putin has signed a decree giving the government powers to temporarily take control of “critical infrastructure” across the country, if private owners fail to protect it from escalating Ukrainian attacks. The new measure comes as Moscow and Kyiv ramp up their air campaigns, with Ukrainian strikes deep into Russian territory sparking fuel shortages and bringing the war closer to home for ordinary Russians. Kyiv has stepped up attacks in recent days on Ozon logistics hubs in Russia – a competitor to the frequently targeted e-commerce giant Wildberries – as it seeks to undermine Moscow’s war-driven economy. The decree, which came into force on Monday, says the new measures are being introduced “in connection with the growing threats to the security of critical infrastructure facilities of the Russian Federation.” It covers a raft of sectors, according to the decree, including fuel and energy infrastructure, communications, transport and logistics facilities, among others. If owners do not take sufficient steps to ensure the “security” of such facilities or restore their functioning quickly enough after attacks, the government can decide to implement “temporary administration,” the decree states. This effectively hands the Russian state control of the owner’s property, property rights and shares. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov on Tuesday said, “quite often the owners of enterprises do not pay proper attention to taking measures to ensure security, anti-drone security.” He also nodded to the support of Western nations for Kyiv as another reason why Moscow “must take measures” to, as he put it, “ensure our own security.” Asked which companies could fall under the remit of the degree, Peskov told reporters the situation would be “analyzed primarily by the government, by the relevant agencies.” “Wherever security measures are not being taken in critical areas, corresponding proposals will be submitted,” he added. Meanwhile, Russia has increasingly been launching high-speed missile attacks across Ukraine, exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of US-made Patriot air defense interceptors, which the country heavily relies upon to shoot down ballistic missiles. It’s a shortage that has been made worse due to a global supply crunch amid the Iran war. Russia launched two missiles and 150 drones at Ukraine overnight into Tuesday, with 124 drones shot down, according to the Ukrainian Air Force. Amid the interceptor shortage, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv had received a “small number of Patriot missiles,” Ukrainian state media outlet Ukrinform reported Tuesday. “I won’t say which country provided them either – we’ve also received a small number of Patriot missiles. I can’t say how many, but just a few. We need more,” Zelensky said in a meeting with his Estonian counterpart, Ukrinform said.

articles.title: Looking for a new job? These are the 10 best US cities for work.
articles.summary: Indeed ranked metros based on job opportunities, compensation, and other factors to determine the best cities for work.
articles.body:
Indeed analyzed US metros with more than 200,000 residents to find the best places for work.

Boston ranked at the top because of its performance across the six categories.

Burlington, Vermont, ranked No. 3, with high scores in opportunities and job quality.

There are several factors beyond salary and the job itself that can make a city a good place for work, said Sneha Puri, an economist at the Indeed Hiring Lab.

That's how the Boston metro area , which has strong career mobility and economic opportunity, ranked at the top of Indeed's new ranking. The job-search platform's Best Cities for Work list was based on an analysis of over 200 metros with more than 200,000 residents. The dozens of metrics used fell into six dimensions: job opportunity, compensation, job quality and security, career mobility and dynamism, work-life and flexibility , and economic opportunity.

Below are the top 10 metros, along with the category that stood out the most.

Puri said the Boston metro area ranked No. 1 because of its "all around balance," ranking fairly well across categories. The metro's highest rank was for career mobility, at No. 2, and its lowest was for job opportunity, at No. 14. Boston employs people in a variety of sectors, with many working in healthcare and professional and business services. Several major colleges and universities are in this metro, including Harvard University , which could be an opportunity for people looking to work in academia or advance their education while working.

Indeed said Boston's robust hybrid work opportunities can help employers attract "elite talent," and that remote and hybrid flexibility "allows workers to find a lifestyle that respects personal time without sacrificing access to high-paying, elite industries or requiring a rigid, traditional 9-to-5 desk presence." Bostonians who enjoy happy hour with colleagues after work or want to grab a bite with friends shouldn't have too much trouble finding somewhere to go. Indeed said the metro ranked No. 10 for restaurant density. Childcare and housing costs were among its weakest-performing metrics.

Puri said the Washington, DC , metro performed strongly in some pillars but less well in others. Puri said its high rank for career mobility and dynamism suggests job seekers shouldn't have too much trouble switching jobs since there are a lot of different employers.

Still, the platform's job postings tracker shows opportunities are below where they were in February 2020. Bureau of Labor Statistics data showed the jobs with the highest share of employment in the metro area, relative to the national employment level, were political scientists, economists, and astronomers.
